The registration page is the form opened by the unique link named “Create an account” from the sign-in page.

The form contains exactly one textbox labeled “Username”, one textbox labeled “Email”, one password input labeled “Password”, one password input labeled “Confirm password”, one initially unchecked checkbox named “Agree to the terms”, and one enabled button named “Create account”.
The username and email identify the account, while passwords must not be echoed on the page.
This product directly marks the email of a successfully registered account as verified and does not provide a subsequent email-verification page.
The visitor enters a unique username, email, password, and matching confirmation, checks “Agree to the terms”, and activates “Create account”.

The username must consist of 1 to 39 lowercase ASCII letters, digits, or single hyphens (`-`) and must not begin or end with a hyphen; after trimming leading and trailing whitespace, the email must contain exactly one `@`, be no longer than 254 characters, and have at least one dot and non-empty domain labels after the `@`; the password must contain 12 to 128 characters, include at least one uppercase letter, one lowercase letter, one digit, and one non-alphanumeric special character, and contain no whitespace characters.

The system stores a sign-in-capable account together with its verified-email status and enters the sign-in page; if the username or email conflicts, any field is missing, the email format is invalid, the terms are not accepted, the password is noncompliant, or the confirmation does not match, the system retains the username and email input, displays an itemized message beside the corresponding field, and does not create an account.

The corresponding visible field message contains “Username already exists”, “Username format is invalid”, “Email format is invalid”, “Password requirements are not satisfied”, or “Agree to terms is required”, as applicable.
Visitors can use this capability on the account-access page.
The system validates input rules, displays field errors, and prevents duplicate accounts; on success, it directly creates an available account.

Submitting several invalid fields together must show the username, email, password, and missing-terms messages together, rather than revealing only one error per submission; the submit button remains actionable so these messages can be read.
For example, a username beginning with a hyphen, email “not-an-email”, password “short”, confirmation “different”, and unchecked terms produce these field errors and preserve the attempted username.
A duplicate username paired with a different unused email displays “Username already exists” and retains both attempted values.

A successful registration accepts a unique username, its email, and password; the sign-in form is immediately available, accepts that email, and the resulting signed-in username remains visible after reload.
This feature builds on the persisted objects.
The sign-in page is the form on the account-access page containing “Username or email”, “Password”, and “Sign in”.
A “session” is the current-browser login record saved after successful account authentication, represented in the frontend by the upper-right account menu and access to protected pages.
The visitor enters a username or email and a password and submits the form.

The system looks up the account and validates its credentials and availability status; if authentication fails due to an unknown username/email, incorrect password, or unavailable account, the system displays exactly the same generic failure message “Invalid credentials”, does not disclose whether the account exists or which credential was wrong, and does not create a session.

After successful authentication, the system stores a session with a unique session identifier, account identifier, and active status, then redirects to the workspace accessible to that user; the session remains valid after refreshing or reopening the workspace, and subsequent protected organization, repository, and work-item requests must use this session to determine the current user.
The sign-in page exposes a visible “Forgot password” link.
The recovery step displays visibly labeled Email, Verification code, New password, and Confirm password fields and a “Send reset link” or “Reset password” button.
A registered verified email and an unknown email both reach the same recovery step and display the fixed verification code `123456` without requiring email delivery.
A wrong code leaves the original password usable and displays “Verification code is invalid”.
A correct code with matching compliant passwords updates the account and displays “Password updated”.

This feature builds on the persisted objects, opened pages, or authenticated-session context provided by REQ-1-1-2 (Sign In with an Existing Account); it must reuse that context and keep pages and data consistent after the context changes.
The page contains exactly one button named “Account menu”; its menu contains exactly one link named “Sign out”.
Activating it displays a dialog named “Sign out” with buttons named “Confirm sign out” and “Cancel”.
The dialog explains that sign-out affects only the current browser session.
Only “Confirm sign out” invalidates the session, while “Cancel” or closing the dialog retains the current session and page.

After confirming, refresh, browser back navigation, or directly reopening a previously accessible protected account, repository, or organization page restores an unauthenticated state and displays the “Sign in” link.

This feature builds on the persisted objects, opened pages, or authenticated-session context provided by REQ-1-1-2 (Sign In with an Existing Account); it must reuse that context and keep pages and data consistent after the context changes.

The security form has uniquely labeled password inputs “Current password”, “New password”, and “Confirm password”, and a button “Update password”; submitting an empty current-password field must display the visible application message “Current password is required”.
A failure with an incorrect current password and confirmation “does-not-match” must display the corresponding current-password or confirmation error and leave the old credentials usable.
Each password-change scenario starts with its own verified account in the stated credential state and a different compliant candidate password.

“Password and authentication” is the security page in account Settings used to change the current account credentials; the change affects only the current account's password record and does not alter any other accounts or resources outside the session.
The user must provide the current password, a new password compliant with the REQ-1 password rules, and a character-for-character identical confirmation password; all three fields are required.
The system validates the change, prevents unauthorized updates, and applies the new password to subsequent sign-in attempts.

If the current password is incorrect, the new password is noncompliant, the confirmation does not match, or any field is missing, the system displays the reason in the corresponding field and does not modify the credentials; the applicable visible message is “Current password is incorrect”, “Password confirmation does not match”, or “Current password is required”.
The old password remains valid and the new password must not work for sign-in.

After a successful update, the page displays “Password updated”, the new password is immediately used for subsequent password-based sign-ins, and the old password must no longer work for new sign-ins.
Seed password-change values are `New-password-456!` for the successful update and
`Required-password-789!` for the missing-current-password scenario.
The organization page presents “Repositories” as a navigation link, visually usable as a tab, and a textbox labeled “Find a repository”.
Filtering updates the visible results as the user types, without a separate submit action.
Each result has a link named exactly with the repository name, and opens a heading displaying “organization name/repository name”.
Returning with browser Back keeps the public result available; filtering by the exact private repository name never exposes its link to a visitor.
The seed organization has a public repository and a distinct private repository inaccessible to visitors.

From the organization page, the user clicks the “Repositories” link, can enter a repository name in the filter box, select a public/private filter, and click a repository name in the list to open its overview.
The system displays only the names, descriptions, visibility, and update times of repositories visible to the current user; clicking a result opens that repository's overview.

Visitors can view public repositories on a public organization overview page; signed-in accounts can see only repositories for which they have read permission on the Repositories tab of the organization overview.

The list reads repository name, description, visibility, and update time and provides no write operations; private repositories must first be validated under the already defined repository-access rules.
The authenticated account menu exposes a visible “Your organizations” link, whose page exposes a visible “New organization” link.
The organization creation page displays visibly labeled “Organization name” and “Display name” fields and a button named “Create organization”.
A signed-in verified account can submit a unique organization identifier and display name; successful creation opens the new organization overview and persists it across reload.
Organization identifiers must be 1–39 lowercase ASCII characters and globally unique.
The display name must contain 1–100 non-whitespace characters after trimming.
A duplicate identifier displays “Organization name already exists” without opening the existing organization.
An invalid identifier displays “Organization name format is invalid”, and a whitespace-only display name displays “Display name is required”; rejected submissions do not create an organization.
The organization overview exposes a visible “Teams” link.
The Teams page exposes a visible “New team” link, which opens a form with a visibly labeled “Team name” field and a “Create team” button.
An organization Owner can submit a unique team name containing 1–50 lowercase ASCII letters, digits, or hyphens, with no leading or trailing hyphen.
A successful submission opens the new team overview and the team heading remains visible after reload.
A malformed team name displays “Team name is invalid” and does not create a team.
An organization Owner can open a team in the organization’s “Teams” page.
The team page exposes “Members” and “Settings”.

On Members, “Add member” opens a visibly labeled “Username” textbox and an “Add member” button; after a valid organization member is added, the member appears in the list with a “Remove <username>” button.
Removing the member updates the list immediately and remains effective after reload.
On Settings, “Parent team” is a combobox and “Save” persists a parent-team change.
A change that would make a team its own ancestor is rejected with “Cyclic team hierarchy is not allowed”, and the previously saved parent remains selected after reload.
An organization Owner can open the organization’s “People” page and click “Add member”.
The form displays a visibly labeled “Username or email” field, a “Role” combobox with a “Member” option, and an “Add member” button.
Adding a registered non-member directly creates the organization membership with Member role, displays the account in People without a pending-invitation state, and persists after reload.
After the member signs in, the organization appears in “Your organizations”, but membership alone does not grant access to an otherwise unauthorized private repository.
Adding an existing member displays “Account is already a member” without duplicating the relationship; an unknown username displays “Account not found”.
The organization overview exposes a “People” link listing member usernames.
For an Owner, a member row exposes a button named “Member menu <username>”; the menu contains “Remove from organization”, followed by a confirmation button named “Remove”.
Confirmed removal removes the member from People immediately and after reload.
A non-Owner can view the member but has no “Member menu <username>” button and no “Remove from organization” menu item.
A repository Admin can open “Settings” and “Manage access”.
“Add people or teams” opens a picker with a visibly labeled “Search” textbox, selectable team options, a “Role” combobox, and an “Add” button.
Adding a team with Write access displays the exact team name and Write role, and the grant remains visible after reload.

An existing access row exposes a “Role” combobox and “Save” button; changing its role from Write to Read updates the existing record rather than creating a duplicate, and exactly one Read row remains after reload.

The top global search control has searchbox role and accessible name “Search”; entering a repository name and pressing Enter displays repository results directly, without requiring an additional type-filter click.
Each repository result has a link whose accessible name is exactly its repository name, while the result also displays its owner/name metadata.
Clicking it opens a heading containing the repository name; reloading preserves that overview.
A query with no matching repository displays “No results”, including when the visitor returns home and repeats the same query.
Seed data provides a named public repository and a private repository inaccessible to visitors; searching the private name exposes no result link for it.
Visitors or signed-in users can search repositories they are authorized to view.
The system accepts a search query, applies repository-oriented filters or scope constraints, and displays matching repositories with sufficient metadata for the user to open the target repository.

This feature builds on the persisted objects, opened pages, or authenticated-session context provided by REQ-1-1-2 (Sign In with an Existing Account); it must reuse that context and keep pages and data consistent after the context changes.
The signed-in workspace provides a “New repository” link.
The form labels are “Owner”, “Repository name”, and “Description”; the signed-in user's personal namespace is selected by default, so it is possible to submit without changing the owner.
Visibility choices are radio controls “Public” and “Private”; initialization is a checkbox “Add a README file”; submission uses the button “Create repository”.
Other defaults must allow duplicate-name and empty-name validation without further input.
A successful initialized private repository shows a heading containing the new name, a visible Private marker, and a README file link; the overview persists after reload.
The optional description “Repository created by Playwright” is saved when entered.
An existing repository in this same default personal namespace is supplied for duplicate validation, which stays on the form and does not open the existing repository heading.

On the repository-creation page, a signed-in user selects a personal or organization owner, enters a repository name and description, selects public or private visibility, and chooses whether to create an initial commit with a README.

The system verifies that the user may create a repository in that owner's namespace, that the name is unique, and that the options are valid; on success, it stores the repository identifier, owner, visibility, default branch, and creator.
If initialization is selected, it must also atomically create the initial branch, README file, and initial commit; failure at any step must leave no partially created repository.
On success, the new repository overview page is opened.
The source overview has a button “Fork”.

The fork form contains a field labeled “Repository name” and button “Create fork”; it defaults to the signed-in user's personal namespace and an allowed visibility, permitting submission after editing only the name.
Seed data supplies a readable source, a user allowed to create personal repositories, and an existing fork name in that namespace for the conflict case.
Success opens a heading containing the new fork name and visible text “Forked from <source repository name>” with a source link; the heading and source relationship survive reload.
On the source repository page, the user clicks “Fork”, selects a target personal or organization namespace, enters an optional new name and visibility, and clicks “Create fork”.
The system creates an independent fork, copies the accessible default-branch history, records the source-repository link, and then opens the new fork overview page.

This feature builds on the persisted objects, opened pages, or authenticated-session context provided by REQ-3-3 (View a Public Repository Overview) and REQ-1-1-2 (Sign In with an Existing Account); it must reuse that context and keep pages and data consistent after the context changes.

A signed-in user can fork only when they have Read or higher permission on the source repository and permission to create repositories in the target personal or organization namespace; when the source repository is private, the fork must remain Private, while a public source repository may be forked as Public or Private.

The system validates permissions on both ends and stores the new fork's owner, visibility, source-repository identifier, default branch, and copied accessible history; if any check fails, no fork is created.
The fork conflict seed uses the existing name `acme-docs-fork` in the target
personal namespace.
On a public repository overview, the “Code” button opens a clone popover with “HTTPS” and “SSH” tabs.
Each tab provides a button for copying the selected clone value.
With browser clipboard permission, the visitor can copy the selected value, receives brief “Copied” feedback, and continues to see the repository heading.
This read-only operation does not modify the repository.
The capability builds on the public repository overview provided by REQ-3-3 (View a Public Repository Overview) and is available to a visitor who can view that repository.
The repository overview identifies a seeded public repository in a visible heading, displays a “Public” marker, and provides a navigation link “Code” distinct from the clone-menu Code button.
The public repository is readable without sign-in and retains its heading after reload.
A repository administrator can open Settings and General, choose Public in the visibility confirmation flow, and activate the confirmation button.
The repository then displays a Public marker and remains readable to an unauthenticated visitor.
A distinct non-admin collaborator can open the same repository, but must not see an actionable Change visibility button.
The visibility change is persisted for the later collaborator check.
This feature builds on the public repository overview provided by REQ-3-3 (View a Public Repository Overview).
A visitor with repository-view permission can use the Code page to browse the selected branch's directory hierarchy and open files without changing repository data.

Directory and file entries are links with their exact accessible names; a directory identifies the current path and a file page displays the stored file name, path, branch context, and readable content.
Seed data provides public repository `acme-docs`, directory `src`, text file `README.md`, and expected content `Document search flow`.
Opening the directory and then the file displays that content, and reloading the file page preserves the same read-only content.
This feature builds on the repository and file browsing context provided by REQ-4-1 (Browse Repository Files and Directories).
A user with repository-view permission can open the repository's commit history from its repository page and inspect the records for the readable branch.
Each record represents an immutable change and may expose its commit identifier, author, time, parent, and changed files.
The repository page exposes a history link named “Commits”; a commit count may accompany the label without creating another matching link.
Seed history includes the message `Document search flow`, author `alice-dev`, and a relative timestamp containing “ago”.
Opening branch history directly displays these values without requiring file editing or other write actions.
This feature builds on the read-only history context provided by REQ-4-2-1 (View Repository Commit History).
A user with repository-view permission can inspect the difference represented by a readable commit and its parent revision.
The comparison is read-only: it displays changed files and numeric additions and deletions without creating a review, comment, commit, or branch change.

Seed data provides an accessible commit entry in public repository `acme-docs` and changed file `src/search.ts`; opening that entry displays the changed-file path, a “Changed files” summary, and numeric additions and deletions.
This feature builds on the repository browsing context provided by REQ-4-1 (Browse Repository Files and Directories).
A visitor can search readable file content within public repository `acme-docs` using the repository Search box, press Enter, and select the “Code” results view.
Search is read-only and remains scoped to the current repository; it does not create commits or modify files.
The results view provides matching file entries and opens a selected file in its repository context.
Seed data provides query `search flow`, matching file `README.md` with that text visible, and absent query `no-such-token`.
A matching file displays the query text and retains its file link after reload.
An absent query displays a no-code-results state and retains the exact query in Search; repeating that search from the repository produces the same empty state.
This feature builds on the repository Code page provided by REQ-4-1 (Browse Repository Files and Directories).
Any user with repository-view permission can use the branch selector to list and switch the branches available to the current repository.
The current branch is reflected consistently by the selector, page entry, and file list; selecting a branch changes the browsing snapshot without creating a commit or rewriting branch history.
The selector is a unique button named “Branch <current branch name>”; it opens a textbox named “Find branch” and selectable options whose exact accessible names are branch names.
As the user types, matching options or a “No matching branch” state update without requiring Enter or a separate search action.
Seed data provides public repository `branch-switch-demo`, active branch `main`, target branch `feature-search`, target-only file `main-only.md`, and unknown query `missing-branch`.
Selecting `feature-search` immediately updates the selector and exposes the target-only file.
Escape closes the selector; an unmatched query leaves the active branch unchanged, including after reload.
A signed-in user with Write, Maintain, Admin, or organization Owner permission can create a named branch from the current branch head through the branch selector.

As the user types, a valid unused name exposes an option named “Create branch: <name>”; selecting it creates the reference and switches the browsing context to the new branch without a second mandatory confirmation.
The new branch points to the selected base commit and does not copy files or rewrite the base branch history.
Read and Triage users may browse but cannot create branches.

Branch names are 1–255 characters and may contain ASCII letters, digits, `-`, `_`, `.`, and `/`; names ending in `/` or `.`, containing `..` or `//`, duplicating an existing name, or submitted by an unauthorized user must be rejected.
The selector and `Find branch` textbox use the controls defined by REQ-4-3-1.
Reloading a successfully created branch preserves it as the selected branch.
A repository Admin or organization Owner can change the default branch from Settings → Branches.
The “Default branch” native select exposes existing branch names as options; selecting a different branch and activating “Update” opens a confirmation flow, and “Confirm” saves the choice.
The default branch is the branch shown when the repository is opened without an explicit branch; changing it does not delete or rewrite the previous branch, its commits, or its files.
Read, Triage, and other non-administrator users may view repository content but must not receive an actionable default-branch combobox or update button.
The saved setting is associated with the repository and remains effective after reopening.
This feature builds on repository browsing and sign-in provided by REQ-4-1 (Browse Repository Files and Directories) and REQ-1-1-2 (Sign In with an Existing Account).
From a writable Code page, a contributor can use “Add file” → “Create new file” to add a file on the current branch.
Only Write, Maintain, Admin, or organization Owner may submit file changes;
Read and Triage may browse but may not write.
A successful submission creates one commit containing the path, content, commit message, author, parent commit, and target branch, then advances that branch head.
The editor exposes a “File name” field, a “File contents” textbox, a “Commit message” field, and a “Commit changes” button.
New file paths cannot be empty, start with `/`, contain a `..` path segment, or conflict with an existing file or directory.
Commit messages must contain 1–72 non-empty characters after trimming whitespace.

Invalid submissions must leave file data, branch head, and commit history unchanged; an invalid path is reported as “Invalid file path”, while a missing message is reported as “Commit message is required”.
Seed data provides public repository `file-management-demo` and Write contributor `file-contributor`.

A valid unique file such as `pw-file-<unique suffix>.md`, nonempty content, and message `Add <file name>` produce a file view containing the saved content; the file's “Commits” link exposes the submitted message.
This feature builds on the public repository overview provided by REQ-3-3 (View a Public Repository Overview).
Users with repository-view permission can read issue rows for the current repository on the Issues list page.
“Open” and “Closed” are links that select status views, and the unique searchbox named “Search issues” filters matching rows as the user types without requiring Enter or a separate search button.
Each result title is a link whose exact accessible name is the title.
Filtering is read-only and does not modify issue data.
Seed data provides public repository `acme-docs`, an Open issue titled `Improve onboarding`, and a Closed issue titled `Legacy welcome text`.
The Open filter plus the known open title continues to show the matching issue after reload; the Closed filter plus the known closed title shows the closed issue and excludes the open issue.
The issue detail page is the read view for one uniquely numbered work item within a repository.
Its heading exposes the complete issue title without the issue number, and the page displays the current Open or Closed status, the complete saved description, and discussion or activity content.
Repository-view permission is sufficient to read this saved data; editable controls are available only to roles authorized for the corresponding operation.
The seeded public repository `acme-docs` contains the Open issue `Improve onboarding` with description `Describe the onboarding improvement.` and discussion or activity text.
Opening the issue from a visible issue entry, reloading its detail page, or reopening it from the application home page preserves the same title, description, and status.
A signed-in user with issue-write permission opens the current repository's
Issues page and follows the `New issue` link.
The form has fields labeled
`Title` and `Description` and a `Submit new issue` button.
A valid submission
stores the repository, title, optional description, author, creation time, and
Open status, assigns a unique repository-scoped number, and opens the new issue
detail page.
The exact entered title is used as the detail heading and issue-list
link, and the exact description is visible.
A title containing only whitespace
is rejected with a title-required message and creates no issue.
Only a signed-in user with Write, Maintain, or Admin may use the unique `Edit issue title` and `Edit issue description` buttons.
The title form has `Issue title` and `Save issue title`; the description form has `Issue description` and `Save issue description`.
Each save updates only its selected field and persists the new value.
Empty titles are rejected, the original value is retained, and reload shows the unchanged original title.
The separate invalid edit seed is an issue titled `Original issue title`.
Only a signed-in user with Write, Maintain, or Admin may enter a non-empty comment on the issue detail page.
The editor is labeled `Comment` and the submit button is named exactly `Comment`.
On success, the system stores the issue, author, body, and creation time, displays the complete text and author username in a discussion article, and preserves it after reload.
Whitespace-only text is rejected or prevented from submission and must not add a comment or timeline entry.
A user with issue-management permission can open the `Assignees` button on an issue detail page.

A user with issue-management permission can use the `Labels` button on an issue detail page.

Selecting an option immediately saves the issue-label relationship without a separate Save action.

A user with issue-management permission can use the `Milestone`

The selector does not create a milestone or associate
one from a different repository.
Only users with Triage, Maintain, or Admin permission may close or reopen an issue from its detail view;
Write and Read users may view status but cannot use either transition control.
Closing stores Closed status and a closure activity without changing the title, description, comments, labels, assignees, or milestone.
An Open issue provides a `Close issue` button; a Closed issue provides a `Reopen issue` button.
Each action saves immediately.
After reopening and reload, the issue is Open and `Close issue` is available again.
Every scenario provides independent seed state and authentication.

A repository Admin can open Settings and Branches, create a rule with `Branch
name pattern`, `Require 1 approval`, and `Require status check test`, and see it

Each scenario has independent accounts and seed state.

A signed-in contributor can use the New pull request comparison page.
Base and Compare comboboxes select branches and `Compare changes` displays the

`Commits` and `Files changed` are links that show commit information and a changed-files summary for the same PR.
The overview remains available after reload or reopening it from the home page; viewing does not mutate PR data.
`Files changed` is the read-only aggregate diff view for a PR.
A public PR can

On an eligible PR, Merge pull request and then Confirm merge are buttons; confirming displays Merged, and that state remains after reload.
A blocked PR keeps a visible disabled Merge pull request button and explains its unmet review or protection condition before any click.
Seed data supplies a Maintain account and separate Open PRs for success and refusal.
The eligible PR targets protected main, has a current non-author approval and test: success, and has no conflicts.
The blocked PR targets a protected branch and lacks the required valid approval; its disabled button is accompanied by Review required by branch protection.
The success and refusal states are separate PR records, so neither test relies on restoring a mutation from the other.
“Merge” is the only write operation that writes the current compare commit's changes from an Open PR into the base branch; it is not simply marking the PR as complete.

Only Maintain, Admin, or organization Owner may merge from the PR detail page using the sole supported “Create a merge commit” method; the merge confirmation area should display satisfied and unsatisfied conditions.

Before confirmation, the system rereads the target branch head, current compare commit, merge-conflict state, and protection rules — there must be no valid Request changes; if the target is protected, each enabled rule requirement is enforced independently, requiring 1 valid non-author Approve for the current compare commit when Require 1 approval is enabled and requiring `test` success when Require status check test is enabled.

Merged is terminal.

This feature builds on the persisted objects, opened pages, or authenticated-session context provided by REQ-6-3-4 (Submit a Pull Request Review) and REQ-6-1 (Protect Branches with Review and Status-Check Requirements); it must reuse that context and keep pages and data consistent after the context changes.
The PR page provides Close pull request and Reopen pull request as buttons for authorized users.
Close pull request immediately sets Closed without an extra confirmation dialog, then Reopen pull request immediately restores Open.
After reload, Close pull request is available again.
For a viewer who is neither author nor Maintain/Admin/Owner, both controls are absent, rather than merely disabled or rejected after activation.
Seed data supplies the author and a separate Read viewer, an authored Open PR for the close/reopen cycle, and a separate Open PR readable by that viewer for permission validation.

When the proposed change should not proceed, the PR author, Maintain, Admin, or organization Owner may close an unmerged Open or Draft PR without merging; the same roles may reopen a Closed PR as Open.

The system stores the status, operator, and time and records the transition, while keeping the PR discussion, reviews, diff, and branch references viewable; closing or reopening must not update any branch.
Merged is terminal, the page does not display close or reopen operations, and the server rejects status changes.

This feature builds on the persisted objects, opened pages, or authenticated-session context provided by REQ-6-2-3 (Create a Pull Request from Comparison Results) and REQ-1-1-2 (Sign In with an Existing Account); it must reuse that context and keep pages and data consistent after the context changes.
This product is a simplified GitHub collaboration platform.

Unless an atomic requirement explicitly allows more than one role, every quoted user-interface name is the exact English accessible name of the control; the role, scope, and observable-state rules stated by each atomic requirement are authoritative.
Values described as existing accounts, organizations, teams, repositories, branches, files, commits, issues, milestones, pull requests, reviews, and permission relationships are predefined seed data.

The application must provision those records before the corresponding scenario and supply each account through an isolated browser session; they are not extra features that a participant must expose through a private API.
Generated names may contain a unique suffix, but their role, ownership, visibility, and relationships are exactly those stated in the atomic requirement.
Every atomic requirement remains enabled even when seed configuration is incomplete.

Organization Owner, repository Admin, Read, Triage, Write, Maintain, and Admin permissions follow the operation-specific rules in the requirements below; these roles are not an automatic cumulative ladder.
Real-time collaboration, Actions, Packages, Wiki, project boards, notification delivery, and external Git remote protocols are outside the scope of this product.
This module defines the “account” and “session” required to access the system.

An account is a persistent individual identity storing a username, verified email, and credential status; a session is a record created after successful account sign-in that represents only the current browser login state.
Visitors enter the account-access page from “Sign up”, “Sign in”, or “Forgot password” on the home page; signed-in users enter security settings or sign out from the account menu.
The account menu is the control in the upper-right corner of the page that displays the current signed-in account, organization list, and sign-out entry.
No page, error message, or recovery flow may display a full password.

After successful sign-in, the account menu displays the current user, and subsequent organization, repository, issue, and pull-request pages use this session to determine visibility and operation permissions; sign-out, password changes, and recovery must immediately change the session state visible to subsequent requests.

The account-access page is the shared page used by unauthenticated users to register, sign in, and recover a password, with the frontend showing the appropriate form and submit button for each operation.

The local product does not implement an email-verification page, email delivery, or an external verification-code service — successful registration directly stores a sign-in-capable account and marks its email as verified; successful sign-in only stores a new session and does not create a duplicate account; after submitting an email for password recovery, the page directly displays the fixed verification code `123456` and the password-reset form, and only the correct code together with a compliant new password updates the password of the same account.

Registration, sign-in, and recovery pages must use visible labels to identify fields and submit actions; after failure, non-sensitive input is retained, while password and password-confirmation fields must not redisplay submitted values.

Signed-in users enter the organization list through “Your organizations” in the account menu and can create or open an organization; visitors can only view public repositories through public organization pages.
The organization overview provides Repositories, People, and Teams entries.
An organization Owner directly adds or removes members on People, creates teams and maintains hierarchy on Teams, and grants roles to members or teams in Manage access under repository Settings.

Organization membership only determines whether a user can see the organization and can be a candidate for team/repository authorization; it does not automatically grant access to any private repository.
Access to a private repository comes only from organization Owner status, a direct role grant on that repository, or direct membership in a team authorized for that repository.
All changes must be reflected simultaneously in organization details, people/team lists, and the actual access results of affected repositories.
The organization overview page uses the organization name as a heading; its “Repositories”, “People”, and “Teams” navigation entries have link roles even when visually styled as tabs.
The Repositories tab lists repositories owned by the organization, the People tab lists members and their Member/Owner roles, and the Teams tab lists teams.
This module supports visitors discovering an organization's public repositories and signed-in accounts creating organizations from the “Your organizations” page.

The unique organization name uses the same globally unique 1–39-character lowercase ASCII format as the REQ-1 username; the display name must contain 1–100 non-empty characters after trimming leading and trailing whitespace.

After successful creation, the system stores the organization object and the creating account's Owner membership relationship, and the user enters the new organization overview page; subsequent team, member, and organization-repository authorization is scoped by this organization identifier.

This feature builds on the persisted objects, opened pages, or authenticated-session context provided by REQ-1-1-2 (Sign In with an Existing Account); it must reuse that context and keep pages and data consistent after the context changes.
On the current organization's member- and team-management pages, users create teams, maintain team hierarchy and membership relationships, and directly add or remove organization members.

A team name contains 1–50 lowercase ASCII letters, digits, or hyphens, may not begin or end with a hyphen, and must be unique within the same organization; a team must belong to an organization, and a parent team must belong to the same organization and may not create a direct or indirect cycle.

Organization membership and team membership are independent persisted relationships; team hierarchy is used only for display and management and does not implicitly add members of a parent or child team to the other team.

On the People page, an Owner enters the username or verified email of an existing account and confirms, after which the system immediately saves that account's Member or Owner membership relationship; there is no invitation, Pending, or acceptance step.

When removing a member, the system atomically deletes that organization-membership relationship, all of that account's team memberships in the organization, and all direct grants to that account on repositories of the organization; team grants themselves are not deleted.

If removal would leave the organization with no Owner, the system rejects the operation and keeps all relationships unchanged; the person's account, personal repositories, and relationships with other organizations must not be deleted.

This feature builds on the persisted objects, opened pages, or authenticated-session context provided by REQ-2-1-2 (Create an Organization After Authentication); it must reuse that context and keep pages and data consistent after the context changes.
A repository is a container for code, branches, commits, files, and collaborative work items.

The repository overview page is titled “owner/repository name”, displays the owner, name, Public/Private marker, description, and default branch, and provides Code, Issues, Pull requests, and Settings entries; the “owner” is an individual account or organization, and a repository belonging to an organization is an organization repository.

Users open a repository overview from global search results, a personal/organization Repositories list, or a direct link; signed-in users with creation permission create a personal or organization repository from “New repository”.

Public repositories allow visitor Read access; private personal repositories allow access only to their owner and explicitly authorized subjects; private organization repositories allow access only to organization Owners, members with direct repository roles, or direct members of teams with repository roles, and ordinary organization Members do not automatically gain access merely through membership.
After visibility or access grants change, search, lists, direct links, and repository pages must all use the same access rule.
The repository-creation page is the form opened by “New repository”, where the user selects an owner, name, visibility, and initialization options.

A “fork” is an independent repository copied from a readable source repository — the frontend displays the source link on the fork overview page, and the system stores the source-repository identifier; branches and commits in the fork may evolve independently and never write back to the source repository.
A “clone page entry” is a read-only address displayed in the repository Code popover and can be copied to the clipboard; it does not mean this product implements an external Git protocol.
Both new repositories and forks must enter a browsable repository overview page.

This feature builds on the persisted objects, opened pages, or authenticated-session context provided by REQ-1-1-2 (Sign In with an Existing Account); it must reuse that context and keep pages and data consistent after the context changes.

The Code page is the main page for browsing code in a repository — the top of the page displays the current branch selector, the main area displays files and directories at the current path on the current branch, clicking a file opens a read-only file page, and clicking Commits opens commit history.
A file is content at a path on a branch; a directory is only a path hierarchy used for organization and is not an independent collaboration object.
A branch is a named reference pointing to a commit, and switching branches only changes the file snapshot read by the current page.

A commit is an immutable change record that stores the parent commit, author, message, time, and changed files; users with Write, Maintain, Admin, or organization Owner permission can create new commits from a file page through Edit or Add file.
Every file, commit, comparison, and branch page displays the repository and current branch or revision.
Editing a file must create a new commit and must not rewrite historical content.

Seed data for read-only scenarios consists of public repositories and directly openable repository, file, and commit pages; visitors need not sign in to browse files, history, diffs, code search, or existing branches.

Write scenarios provide separate existing contributor accounts with Write or higher permission on their target repositories and an unprotected writable branch; default-branch scenarios provide an Admin and a separate readable non-Admin account.

These accounts sign in through the home-page “Sign in” link, the “Username or email” and “Password” fields, and the “Sign in” button; the signed-in username is visible before opening the target repository entry.
Unless a narrower scope is explicitly given below, each named control is unique on the active page, and field and option names refer to accessible names.

The “commit history” page displays commit records for a branch or file path in reverse chronological order; the “diff” page compares the file contents of two commits or revisions line by line, where base is the earlier or target revision and compare is the newer or to-be-compared revision; the “code search” page searches for keywords only within readable file content in the current repository.
All three are read-only views that do not create commits or modify files or branches and follow repository visibility and access permissions.

This feature builds on the persisted objects, opened pages, or authenticated-session context provided by REQ-4-1 (Browse Repository Files and Directories); it must reuse that context and keep pages and data consistent after the context changes.
The branch selector is the control at the top of the Code page that lists and switches branches; the system stores a unique name and current pointed-to commit for each branch.
Creating a branch creates a new named reference at a specified base commit; it does not copy files or rewrite base history.
The default branch is the branch read by default when opening the repository overview or a repository entry without a specified branch; it is not the only existing or writable branch.

A branch name is 1 to 255 characters and may contain only ASCII letters, digits, `-`, `_`, `.`, and `/`; it must not end with `/` or `.`, and must not contain consecutive `..` or `//`; duplicate names, invalid names, or lack of permission must prevent branch creation.
Changing the default branch must not alter existing branches, commits, or source/target references of already-open PRs.

This feature builds on the persisted objects, opened pages, or authenticated-session context provided by REQ-4-1 (Browse Repository Files and Directories); it must reuse that context and keep pages and data consistent after the context changes.
An issue is a persistent work item within a repository used to record pending work, a defect, or a discussion topic; it is not a code file or PR.

The Issues page is the list page in repository navigation; each row displays the issue number, title, Open/Closed status, author, and labels, and clicking the number or title opens the issue detail page.

At the top of the detail page are the title and status; the right side displays Assignees, Labels, and Milestone metadata in order; the main area displays the description, comments, and activity timeline.
The “activity timeline” is an append-only history that records creation, edits, comments, assignment, labels, milestone, and status changes in chronological order.

A label is a pre-existing colored classification name in the current repository; a milestone is a pre-existing goal-classification item in the current repository that may be associated with multiple issues or PRs but does not change their content or status.
Write, Maintain, and Admin may create issues, edit titles/descriptions, and comment;
Triage, Maintain, and Admin may assign participants, apply labels, set milestones, and close or reopen issues;
Read may only view.

Every operation is performed around a unique issue number within the repository, and the detail page and list display the same persisted data; after refresh, re-login, or opening from another account with view permission, the same record is still read.
For issue operations, the explicit role lists in this module define eligibility per operation rather than an implicit cumulative grant from a role's name;
Write can create, edit, and comment but cannot assign, label, set milestones, or change status.
Organization Owners act with Admin permission.

Read-only seed scenarios provide a public repository's visible Issues entry, distinct Open and Closed issues with known titles, and an issue entry with known title, description, metadata, and discussion.

Mutation scenarios provide isolated issues for successful editing, invalid-title editing with a known original title, commenting, comment validation, assignment, labels, milestone, and closing; their initial states must not be changed by another scenario.
The author and commenter accounts have Write or higher permission; the editor used for both content and metadata operations has Maintain or Admin permission.
A separate viewer has Read permission on a protected issue.
All authenticated scenarios use the home-page “Sign in” link, fields labeled “Username or email” and “Password”, and the “Sign in” button, after which the signed-in username is visible.
Named controls below are unique on the active page unless a narrower scope is stated; detail pages and reloads must work independently of earlier list navigation.
The Issues list page displays the persisted work items for the current repository.
Status and keyword filters change only the rows displayed in the browser and do not create, update, or delete issues.
Each issue row identifies a repository-scoped issue and may display its number, title, Open/Closed status, author, labels, and update time.

The issue detail page is the complete read view of one issue: it displays the issue number, title, status, saved description, metadata such as assignees, labels, and milestone, and discussion or activity records.
Users with repository-view permission may read this information; editing and other mutation controls are governed by the corresponding role requirements.
This feature builds on the public repository overview provided by REQ-3-3 (View a Public Repository Overview) and keeps list and detail views consistent after navigation or reload.
Supports creating issues in the current repository, editing titles and descriptions, and appending discussion comments.

An issue title contains 1-256 non-empty characters after trimming leading and trailing whitespace; the description may be empty and is at most 65536 characters; a comment contains 1-65536 non-empty characters after trimming leading and trailing whitespace.

A successful creation receives a unique repository-scoped number and Open status; editing changes only the selected field of the target issue; comments are appended as independent discussion records with their author and timestamp.
Required-field validation and persistence failures must leave the affected issue or discussion unchanged.
Each scenario supplies its own authenticated account and issue context, so it does not require a previous scenario to run.
An assignee is a repository member associated with an issue; a label is a repository-scoped classification; and a milestone is a repository-scoped planning target.
These metadata relationships do not change repository permission.
Users with Triage, Maintain, or Admin permission may modify them, while other users may view the saved metadata only.
Selecting an available option saves the relationship immediately; reload displays the saved state.
Each scenario provisions its own account, target issue, and selectable repository-scoped metadata.
A pull request (PR) is a persistent proposal to “merge code changes from the compare branch into the base branch”; it is not a branch, commit, or issue.
The Pull requests page lists the current repository's PR number, title, author, source/target branches, and status;

“New pull request” first opens the comparison page, where the user selects base (the target branch that receives the changes) and compare (the source branch that provides the changes) and inspects the diff.
On the PR detail page, Conversation displays the title, description, ordinary comments, activities, and review summary;
Commits displays commits on the compare branch relative to base;
Files changed displays per-file, per-line differences;
Checks displays check status for the PR's current compare commit.

A PR's persisted status may only be Draft, Open, Closed, or Merged — normal creation produces Open, draft creation produces Draft, and the author or Maintain/Admin may mark a Draft as Ready for review to transition it to Open; the author or Maintain/Admin may transition an unmerged Open or Draft PR to Closed and may transition Closed back to Open;
Merged is terminal and cannot be closed or reopened.
Write, Maintain, and Admin may add inline comments and submit reviews, the author or Maintain/Admin may request reviewers, and only Maintain, Admin, or organization Owner may merge.
Each PR stores a repository-scoped number, source/target branches, creation-time and current compare commits, creation-time base commit, title, description, author, status, and activity records.

When the compare branch receives a new commit, the system updates the current compare commit, marks all existing review decisions as stale while preserving them in the timeline, recalculates merge eligibility, and retains inline comments at their original commit and line position marked Outdated.
Failure does not change branches or PR state.
The following REQ-6 interaction contracts use English accessible names and apply to direct navigation as well as navigation from a repository.
Each named action, field, and navigation link is unique on its active page unless explicitly repeated per changed line or reviewer.
PR titles are headings whose accessible name is exactly the persisted title; list titles are links with that same exact name.
Conversation, Commits, Files changed, and Checks are navigation links, even when visually styled as tabs.
The current PR status is visible text.

Signed-in scenarios begin with the unique Sign in link on the home page, labeled Username or email and Password fields, a Sign in button, and the account username visible after authentication; each role account has a username, verified email, and password.
Visitor scenarios use public repositories and require no session.

Seed records identify the corresponding pages, not to private implementation interfaces; role accounts, branches, PRs, and mutable state must be provisioned as distinct records for each stateful scenario; no scenario may rely on a mutation performed by an earlier scenario, and the complete seed set is present before the serial suite starts.
Existing titles, usernames, paths, and branch names described below are supplied as seed values and must be displayed verbatim; generated PR titles and comments may carry a unique suffix.
Supports listing pull requests, comparing source and target branches, and creating normal or draft PRs from a valid comparison.
Public visitors may read PR lists; authenticated users with Write, Maintain, or Admin may create PRs.
Normal PRs start Open, draft PRs start Draft, and an authorized draft author may mark a draft Ready for review.
Each scenario provisions independent accounts, branches, PRs, and mutable state.
A pull request detail page provides read-only overview, Commits, and Files changed views for repository viewers.
A non-author reviewer with Write, Maintain, or Admin permission can add line comments and submit review decisions on an Open PR.
A line comment is anchored to the current changed code and is either published immediately or stored as a pending review comment.
A review stores its reviewer, decision, optional summary, and current compare commit.
Each scenario provisions independent PRs, account roles, changed files, and review state.

preconditions: The username and email identify the account, while passwords must not be echoed on the page.

The username must consist of 1 to 39 lowercase ASCII letters, digits, or single hyphens (`-`) and must not begin or end with a hyphen; after trimming leading and trailing whitespace, the email must contain exactly one `@`, be no longer than 254 characters, and have at least one dot and non-empty domain labels after the `@`; the password must contain 12 to 128 characters, include at least one uppercase letter, one lowercase letter, one digit, and one non-alphanumeric special character, and contain no whitespace characters.

The corresponding visible field message contains “Username already exists”, “Username format is invalid”, “Email format is invalid”, “Password requirements are not satisfied”, or “Agree to terms is required”, as applicable.

Submitting several invalid fields together must show the username, email, password, and missing-terms messages together, rather than revealing only one error per submission; the submit button remains actionable so these messages can be read.
effects: The registration page is the form opened by the unique link named “Create an account” from the sign-in page.

The form contains exactly one textbox labeled “Username”, one textbox labeled “Email”, one password input labeled “Password”, one password input labeled “Confirm password”, one initially unchecked checkbox named “Agree to the terms”, and one enabled button named “Create account”.
The username and email identify the account, while passwords must not be echoed on the page.
This product directly marks the email of a successfully registered account as verified and does not provide a subsequent email-verification page.
The visitor enters a unique username, email, password, and matching confirmation, checks “Agree to the terms”, and activates “Create account”.

The username must consist of 1 to 39 lowercase ASCII letters, digits, or single hyphens (`-`) and must not begin or end with a hyphen; after trimming leading and trailing whitespace, the email must contain exactly one `@`, be no longer than 254 characters, and have at least one dot and non-empty domain labels after the `@`; the password must contain 12 to 128 characters, include at least one uppercase letter, one lowercase letter, one digit, and one non-alphanumeric special character, and contain no whitespace characters.

The system stores a sign-in-capable account together with its verified-email status and enters the sign-in page; if the username or email conflicts, any field is missing, the email format is invalid, the terms are not accepted, the password is noncompliant, or the confirmation does not match, the system retains the username and email input, displays an itemized message beside the corresponding field, and does not create an account.

The corresponding visible field message contains “Username already exists”, “Username format is invalid”, “Email format is invalid”, “Password requirements are not satisfied”, or “Agree to terms is required”, as applicable.
Visitors can use this capability on the account-access page.
The system validates input rules, displays field errors, and prevents duplicate accounts; on success, it directly creates an available account.

Submitting several invalid fields together must show the username, email, password, and missing-terms messages together, rather than revealing only one error per submission; the submit button remains actionable so these messages can be read.
For example, a username beginning with a hyphen, email “not-an-email”, password “short”, confirmation “different”, and unchecked terms produce these field errors and preserve the attempted username.
A duplicate username paired with a different unused email displays “Username already exists” and retains both attempted values.

A successful registration accepts a unique username, its email, and password; the sign-in form is immediately available, accepts that email, and the resulting signed-in username remains visible after reload.
